1 Introduction
Fluid dynamics studies the evolution and dynamics of fluids, both liquid and gaseous.
In general, the distinction between gas and liquids is not so important from the point of
view of fluid dynamics as the distinction between compressible flow and incompressible
flow. From the point of view of thermodynamics, gases and liquids have, as everybody
knows, very different characteristics. In particular, liquids are often treated as if they
are incompressible, i.e. even significant changes in pressure are not capable of causing
significant variations in their density. Very different is the case of gases, which, on the
contrary, are considered compressible fluids. The definition that is used in fluid dynamics
is completely different so that it is not surprising that we can consider incompressible flow
of a compressible fluid. Fluid dynamics defines as incompressible the flows that do not
cause significant variations in density in the fluid. There are several criteria to find out if
a particular flow is compressible or not. The simplest to use is based on Mach’s number,
defined as the ratio between fluid velocity and sound velocity under the same conditions:

different from those reserved for incompressible flows, regardless of whether they are on a
liquid or a gas.
The equations that fluid dynamics use to describe the motion of fluids are based on the
hypothesis that fluid iscontinuous. For most common applications this hypothesis can
be considered acceptable. If we consider that the free path of molecules in the gases is
in the order of10−7m, it is easy to expect that, only if you want a resolution lower than
that scale, the hypothesis of the continuous is acceptable. For liquids, since the average
free path of the molecules is about 3 orders of magnitude lower than that of the gas,
the hypothesis of the continuous is even more applicable. During this Course we always
assume that the hypothesis of continuity is acceptable, since the scales of interest are
larger than those corresponding to the free path of the molecules.
The equations on which the fluid dynamics of reactive systems are based can be divided
into two categories:
1. Balance or conservation equations: equations that express the conservation of total
mass, momentum, and energy. Indeed, through the application of appropriate bal-
ances, it is possible to formulate similar equations, which more properly take the
name of transport equations, for quantities that are not necessarily preserved (such
as the masses of the individual species of a mixture). The most commonly used
transport equations in fluid mechanics are the following:
• individual chemical species (keep in mind that individual atomic elements are
conserved and therefore it is possible to formulate equations of conservation);
• entropy;
• turbulent kinetic energy;
• dissipation rate of turbulent kinetic energy;
• Reynolds Stress Tensor (RST).
2. Constitutive laws: describing quantitatively the physical properties of fluids. The
most important are: the Newton’s law, the Fourier’s law, and the Fick’s law. Also
the equations of state, which express the link between temperature, pressure, and
density of a fluid, fall within this category.
The formulation of the transport equations of different quantities requires the use of some
mathematical tools, which are not the expression or translation of any physical law, but
which find their basis only on geometric aspects of fluid flow (kinematic theorems). The
Leibnitz formula is particularly relevant to express the derivative of an integral with vari-
able limits. Leibnitz’s theorem, also known as the generalized transport theorem, is a
generalization of particular importance to fluid mechanics. Often this theorem is also re-
ferred to as theReynolds transport theorem, to underline its more general character than
the Leibnitz formula.
In general, in order to be able to fully describe a reactive system, it is necessary to be
able to manage the fluid thermodynamics. As everyone knows, thermodynamics is based
on the concept of equilibrium states and assumes that any change in the fluid occurs in an
extremely slow way, so that it goes through equilibrium states. However, the motion of a
fluid in general is not necessarily slow and therefore the laws of classical thermodynamics
could not work (in principle). However, what is done in practice is to assume that a state of
equilibrium is reached locally so that the principles and laws of classical thermodynamics
can be applied.

Of course, the transport equations can not be resolved analytically because of their
complexity (in fact they are partial differential equations or PDEs). Numerical approaches
must therefore be used, which are able to guarantee good accuracy and robustness, and
which will be analyzed in more detail during this Course.
2 Transport Equations
In the following, we will introduce equations describing the behavior of multicomponent
mixtures in a general vector form. The proposed equations can then be expressed in
any reference system (e.g. Cartesian, cylindrical, or spherical) by using mathematical
tools. This ensures that the equations have the same physical meaning, regardless of the
reference system being considered. In general, in the field of computational fluid dynamics,
it should be noted that non-orthogonal curvilinear coordinate systems are often used when
very complex geometries hav to be treated. So having the equations in a form independent
of the coordinate system is of utmost importance.
2.1 Lagrangian vs Eulerian formulations
There are several approaches through which conservation equations (and more generally
transport equartions) can be obtained. First of all, it is appropriate to introduce the
concept of control system and control volume on which the conservation equations are
based. The term control system is used to uniquely identify a set of atoms and molecules
(mass)thatareaveryprecisepartofthematerialbeingconsidered(notnecessarilyafluid);
such a set of atoms and molecules can interact with other control systems surrounding it,
but without exchanging mass with them. A control volume, on the other hand, is a mass-
independent geometric entity, which corresponds to a very precise volume of material, in
principle variable over time. One aspect to be immediately clarified is that in principle
the fluid dynamics equations should be formulated in terms of control system rather than
control volumes. However, from a practical and applicative point of view it is much more
convenient to have equations written on the control volumes and for this reason you have
to be able to switch from one formulation to another. This possibility is guaranteed by
the Reynolds transport theorem(or Leibnitz theorem) in the integral form. In general fluid
mechanics prefers to work in terms of control volumes; structural mechanics in terms of
control system.
There is a particular control volume of great importance, which at the same time also
has the features of a control system and that is defined as thematerial control volume.
With this term, we refer to the volume of fluid that contains always and only the entire
mass of fluid that was present within it at the initial instant. The surface that delimits
this volume is defined ascontrol surface(CS). The material control volume is therefore a
geometric entity, but defined on the mass. When talking about material control volume,
the term Lagrangian is also used. Contrary to Lagrangian’s point of view, there is the
Eulerian’s point of view, which takes into account a fixed volume control in space.
For the derivation of conservation and transport equations, there is noa priori better
solution between the Lagrangian and the Eulerian points of view. The most appropriate
choice depends on the specific features of the problem that you are considering. In prin-
ciple, it is possible to choose volumes of any size and shape. Conceptually, the simplest
possible description of the fluid is represented by the choice of a material control volume
(which is therefore not fixed in space) that moves at the same velocity of the fluid. Though
this is the conceptually more intuitive formulation, it is rarely used since its translation

Conservation and transport equations can be formulated in three equivalent main ap-

A fluid particle that moves in space with a fixed reference system is taken into
account. Then the balance equation is applied on the quantity of interest. This
balance is based on the assumption that the value of any fluid property at the
position r and at timet coincides with that of the infinitesimal particle occupying
the positionr at the instantt. Through the substantial derivative operator (defined
below), one can move from this Lagrangian to the Eulerian formulation.

7 Constitutive laws
Now we want to identify constitutive laws that quantify the diffusion fluxes of species,
energy, and momentum that have been introduced into the corresponding balance equa-
tions. In the conservation equations we saw that it is necessary to express such fluxes as
a function of variables that characterize the fluid, such as temperature, pressure, density
and composition, as well as the physical properties. We will refer hereafter to fluids with-
out memory, for which instantaneous and local state can always be defined in terms of
instantaneous and local variables. We will see, that the diffusive fluxes of the three main
quantities of interest (species, energy, and momentum) have very similar expressions, being
related to the second principle of thermodynamics. Be aware that, unlike the conservation
equations, the constitutive laws we are going to define are the mathematical translation
of empirical observations and therefore the represent models. Thus they can be more or
less detailed. In fact, we will see that constitutive laws can have more terms depending
on the level of detail that you want to reach and depending on the type of problem you
are considering.

8 Classification of flows
Let us go back to the equations of momentum. They are much more complex than they
may seem: indeed they are strongly non-linear, coupled, and difficult to solve. numerically
Moreover, itisextremelydifficulttoprovemathematicallythattheyadmitasinglesolution
with fixed boundary and initial conditions. Experience has shown that Navier-Stokes’
equations are able to describe Newtonian fluids sufficiently accurately in the vast majority
of cases. However, only in a limited number of cases (and in geometries of extreme
simplicity) it is possible to arrive to their analytical solution. These cases are important
for studying some of the fundamental features of fluid flows, but their relevance from the
point of view of application is minimal.
In all cases where an analytical solution is not possible, it is necessary to proceed
according to appropriate numerical methods. However in many cases of practical interest,
some of the terms in the Navier-Stokes equations are null or neglegible, because they
are significantly less important than the rest. Obviously this simplification leads to a
reduction in the mathematical complication of equations, but it also introduces errors.
However, even these simplified equations can be solved analytically only in rare cases,
but the numerical methods that need to be employed are often much simpler than those
required for the complete set of equations. So let us have a look at the most important
simplifications we can consider.
8.1 Incompressible flows
Incompressible flows can characterize both incompressible and compressible fluids (i.e.
both liquid and gaseous fluids): in the first case the compressibility factor of a liquid is
virtually null; in the second case, the incompressible flow hypothesys is only possible if
fluid velocities are sufficiently lower than the propagation speed of the sound (in general
it is required that the Mach number is less than0.30). Special numerical algorithms can
be applied when the hypothesis of incompressible flow is acceptable.
8.2 Inviscid flows (Euler’s equations)
Generally at sufficiently high distances from the walls, the viscosity effects are very small.
If we neglect the effects of viscosity, i.e. we assume the stress tensor is reduced toπ=pδ,
the equations of Navier-Stokes are reduced to so-calledEuler’s equations. The equation
of continuity remains the same, but the equations of conservation of momentum become:
∂ρ
∂t+∇·(ρv) = 0 (196)
ρDv
Dt =−∇p +ρF (197)
Since the fluid is not viscous (we say it is inviscid), there is no friction on the walls,
at which the fluid can flow without any resistance. Euler equations are used study high
speed flows. In these conditions, due to high fluid velocity, viscous effects are important
only in a region of very small thickness on solid surfaces and Euler equations are able to
give a sufficiently accurate representation of the motion of the fluid. The Euler equations
are not in themselves easier than the complete equations, since the nonlinear term (which
is generally more problematic to deal with) remains the same. The advantage is that we
can use much more coarse grids. Only the boundary layer requires a detailed description
of the grid. For example, the study of wing profiles or aerodynamic aspects is performed
through the Euler’s equations.

pages.text:
8.3 Potential flows
Potential flows are the easiest flows to solve. They are simultaneously characterized by
their non-viscous properties (as in Euler equations) and by the fact that the velocity field
is irrotational:
rot (v) = 0 (198)
From this latter condition one can prove the existence of a velocity potentialΦ, such
that the velocity vector can be written as follows:v =−∇Φ.
At the same time, the equation of continuity, assuming a constant density, implies that
∇v = 0. Then combining the two equations, we get a single equation describing the
potential Φ and hence allowing the velocity field to be determined:
∇·(∇v) = 0 (199)
The above equation is a scalar equation (Laplace equation) and allows us to compute
the potential over the computation domain. It can also be written by introducing the
Laplace operator:∇2v = 0. Using the velocity definitionv =−∇Φ then the velocity field
can be determined. It is true that Laplace’s equation, in its simplicity, can not be resolved
analytically unless in particular cases (and still with very simple geometries): however, its
numerical resolution is extremely easy and does not have any particular difficulty. Next to
the velocity potential, it is also possible to define a streamline functionψ, defined in such
a way that the velocity vectors are tangent to the current lines (streamlines); in turn, the
streamlines are orthogonal to the constant potential lines.
Potential flows are extremely interesting in research and theoretical, but they are not
very realistic and therefore of little practical interest.
8.4 Viscous flows (Stokes’ equations)
When the number of Reynolds that characterizes the motion of a fluid is very low (that is,
when the fluid velocity is very low, the viscosity is high and/or the geometry size is very
small) the convective (or nonlinear) term in the Navier-Stokes equations can be neglected.
The flow is dominated by viscous, pressure, and external forces (creeping flow). If the
fluid properties can be considered constant, the equations of conservation of momentum
becomes linear and take the name ofStokes equations:
∂ρ
∂t+∇·(ρv) = 0 (200)
∂(ρv)
∂t =−∇p−∇·τ+ρF (201)
The main advantage is that the non linear term corresponding to convection was com-
pletely removed.
8.5 Boussinesq’s approximation
In reactive flows or in general non-isothermal flows, fluid properties are a function of
temperature, and in particular, the density can not be considered constant and uniform.
However, if density variations are not very high, the density can be treated as if it were
a constant in accumulation and convective terms, and its variability can only be main-
tained in the external term associated with the acceleration of gravity. This is known as
41

pages.text:
Boussinesq approximation, and consists in assuming that the density varies linearly with
the temperature. Then the source term in the equation for conservation of momentum
becomes:
(ρ−ρ0)gi =−ρ0giβ(T−T0) (202)
where βis the coefficient of compressibility. This approximation does not involve any
significant errors if the maximum temperature differences are in the order of10−20◦C..
If the differences were to become higher, then errors could become significant.
8.6 Boundary-layer equations
If the motion of the fluid has a special direction of development (and therefore there are
no recirculation) and the geometry does not show any sharp variation, the flow is almost
exclusively influenced by the upstream fluid. Consider, for example, fluid motion in pipes,
channels, flat or slightly curved surfaces. In these cases we may consider them asboundary
layer flows. In such conditions, Navier Stokes’s equations can be simplified, since:
• diffusive (or viscous) transport of momentum along the main direction is much
smaller than convective transport and it can therefore be neglected;
• the velocity component along the main direction is considerably larger than the
components in the other two directions;
• the pressure gradient component along the main direction is much greater than that
in the other directions.
Without going into details, it can be shown that the boundary layer equations for a two-
dimensional flow are reduced to the following form (in Cartesian coordinates):

9 Classification of Transport Equations
The conservation and transport equations derived in the previous sections require initial
conditions (IC) and boundary conditions (BC) to be solved. Defining these conditions is
a delicate process and must be done with great care. It’s not always easy or even possible
to express initial and boundary conditions accurately, and often significant simplifications
are required. The manner in which these conditions are defined largely depends on the
characteristics of the equations to which they apply. In particular, two categories of
problemscanbedistinguished: stationaryproblems(steady-stateorequilibriumproblems)
and non-stationary problems (unsteady or marching problems, although the latter term
is more general).
9.1 Steady-state (stationary) problems
As implied by the name, problems of this type do not involve the time dependence of
the considered variables and thus represent physical situations where a temporal transient
has been surpassed, leading to a state of equilibrium. Classical stationary problems in
fluid mechanics are governed by elliptic equations. The simplest elliptic equation, which
in some ways can be considered a prototype for more general elliptic equations, is the
Laplace equation (which, for instance, describes the potential of an irrotational Eulerian
flow):
∇2Φ = 0 (210)
where Φ represents a generic variable. The Laplace equation can describe numerous
physical phenomena, such as thermal conduction in solids. In Figure 13, purely for illus-
trative purposes, we have the case of a metal bar with assigned temperatures at the ends,
constant over time. The problem is one-dimensional and is governed by a Laplace equa-
tion: ∂2T

variable (in this case,T) are specified on all boundaries of the computational domain. For
this reason, problems of this type, requiring boundary conditions on all boundaries, are
also referred to as boundary-value problems.
A highly significant characteristic of elliptic problems is that a disturbance at any point
within the computational domain or on its boundaries leads to a change in the solution
at all other points. Therefore, disturbances are said to propagate in all spatial directions.
Additionally, the solution of a problem governed by an elliptic equation never exhibits dis-
continuities; itremainssmoothevenwhendiscontinuitiesmightbe presentinthe boundary
conditions. This aspect is of great importance for the formulation and application of nu-
merical methods to solve the problem. To ensure that information can propagate in all

9.2 Unsteady problems
Non-steady problems naturally involve a temporal evolution of various quantities char-
acterizing fluid motion. Non-steady problems in fluid mechanics can be either parabolic
or hyperbolic. Strictly speaking, a marching problem doesn’t necessarily imply a non-
steady problem. Indeed, some steady motions can be described by parabolic or hyperbolic
equations. Consider, for example, the boundary layer equations, which are derived under
the assumption of the existence of a privileged coordinate for fluid motion that behaves
equivalently to a temporal coordinate, even though it is spatial. For simplicity, we won’t
delve into such problems, and thus, we will use the term "non-steady" (though not entirely
accurately) when referring to parabolic or hyperbolic equations.
Parabolic equations describe non-steady problems that involve significant energy dissi-
pation. The prototype equation of this kind is the diffusion equation:

The equations that govern the motion of fluids at high velocities (with Mach∼1 or

unlike elliptic and parabolic equations, which assume an infinite disturbance velocity.

10 Definition of Boundary Conditions
Based on what was emphasized in the previous section, it is clear that defining boundary
conditions is not a straightforward task due to the complicated and mixed (parabolic,
hyperbolic, and elliptic) nature of transport equations. In fact, there are no general the-
oretical (purely mathematical) guidelines to determine admissible boundary conditions.
Common practice is to identify the most appropriate boundary conditions based on phys-
ical considerations. Table 6 simplifies the common initial and boundary conditions used
for the Navier-Stokes equations and the transport equations of species and energy. The
subscripts n and t indicate the directions normal and tangential to the boundary, andF
represents the assigned stress on the surface.
Note that it is not necessary to specify the density value on the surfaces or outlets,
thanks to the particular nature of the continuity equation. On the contrary, at the inlets,
this value is required. In all other points within the computational domain and on all
other boundaries, the density is the result of the continuity equation and does not require
any boundary condition to be specified (of course, assuming the incompressibility of the
fluid, the density is constant and uniform, so the problem does not arise entirely).
